newsitem.title: ITALY: EU bangs the drum for food aid at summit.
newsitem.headline: EU bangs the drum for food aid at summit.

text.p: The European Union weighed in at the World Food Summit on Friday, advocating a global partnership to fight hunger which recognised that free trade had to be tamed by food aid to the poor.
European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said nations should stop trying to find "scapegoats" for malnutrition and work together to end what he called "a scourge and a curse" on society.

"Citizens in poor populated areas must do more to limit population growth whereas citizens in well-off areas must notably strive to limit over-consumption and accept to contribute personally and through their countries to help the undernourished at home and abroad," Fischler said in a speech to the summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
"External support must complement food security efforts of the net food-importing developing countries," the EU's top farm official added.
"We all know in our hearts that simply liberalising the agricultural market cannot be the only answer, because there are many people who cannot pay."
Cuts in Western food aid rankle with many of the food-importing countries at the summit. They accuse the West of abandoning them to become victims of violent fluctuations in grain prices.
It also divides the biggest food aid donors, the EU and the United States, which have squabbled in the past over the size of their donations.

The EU last year bitterly criticised a U.S. decision to reduce funding for the amount of grain offered as foreign aid. Washington, however, says it always exceeds its minimum pledges and remains the world's leading food aid supplier.

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, pledging support for starving refugees in eastern Zaire, said on Wednesday that Washington remained committed to easing hunger but that free trade was the best way to end the root causes of poverty.
Fischler met Glickman over dinner on Thursday to discuss some of the lingering trade disputes between the two farm giants they did not tackle food export policy, officials said.
German Agriculture Minister Jochen Borchert echoed Fischler's position on trade.

"The liberalisation of trade has its limits, and the agricultural sector is no exception," Borchert said. But he added that future food security "will depend primarily on the developing countries' own efforts".
Baroness Lynda Chalker, Britain's minister for overseas development, said the world should stop having gatherings such as the food summit and take action instead.

"I for one -- and there are many others -- think that implementing action plans for the benefit of our fellow human beings must be at the top of all our agendas, not more summits," she said. "We've had enough of them."
